utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness, who's had protection until giving evidence, is Ante Markovic. I trust the Chamber has a copy of a witness summary that has been signed by him a couple of weeks ago now and has been served on the accused in both English and B/C/S. My request is that, to the extent the Chamber judges it appropriate, the signed statement may stand as his examination-in-chief. Before concluding what I have to say, may I have, well, 30 seconds or a minute in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. We, you know, cannot rule on these summaries to admissibility unless we have them in advance. I've not seen this before sitting down today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, they were certainly sent earlier on my instructions, and Ms. Dicklich tells me they were with your legal officers on Monday, or they were sent to your legal officers on Monday because I had this problem, of course, in mind. And I think I mentioned last week that they either had been served on the accused and were forthcoming, but there was no reason for them not to be available to you a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look into that, but I haven't seen this. What is the -- we could quickly go through it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have two remarks, Mr. May. The document from Igalo has already been produced here. I don't know through which witness, and in public session. It's the document from the meeting when Lord Carrington was there, Veljko Kadijevic and myself, and this document has been under consideration, so it is under no restriction of any kind. However, Mr. Nice, of course, has overlooked this. My second remark, in connection with Jovic's book. I suppose Jovic himself can introduce it. Why should Ante Markovic introduce Jovic's book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only relevance, I guess, are episodes which deal with Mr. Markovic himself, in which case he can -- is in a position to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was certainly my recollection that the Igalo document had been produced. We searched for it last night in the various indices and couldn't find it. That's the reason I've taken the cautious step of seeking it again and then finding it was subject to Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recollect it. I recollect talk of it, because having read my notes, there is talk -- mention of the Igalo agreement. But I do not remember the agreement. It is may be that it is in the -- in some of the Defence documents which were produced to Mr. Samardzic or a witness of that sort, but I don't recollect it. But in any event, a search can be made. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In summary, of course, if I can just explain, of course, Mr. Markovic was the last Prime Minister of the federal -- equivalent to Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He gives an account of, in very summary form, of his years in office, ending in December 1991. And that includes an account of the accused's attitude towards the policies then being pursued, which will be of value in the overall context of the case. He gives an account of the arming of the Bosnian Serbs. You can find that on page 11. He gives a very brief account of the summary of military activity. On page 14, a reference to paramilitaries. Then we come to page 17 to 22, which is a passage -- perhaps the most part of the evidence from the point of view of the trial, because the Chamber is not concerned to -- to determine which political policies are wrong or right, I don't suspect, and you see that there are personal contacts with the accused which are significant in what they reveal of him. And then on page 19, a detailed account of what he was told about Karadjordjevo. That would obviously have to be given live, in any event, as would the meeting in The Hague and the last meeting that he had with the accused. So that in reality much of -- or everything from 17 onwards will have to be given live and there are quite a lot of references or many references to the accused in the earlier passages which I could touch on or deal with in detail as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be a sensible way to go about it so that the evidence could be put into context - and I make this as a suggestion by myself, of course - that you summarise what's in the rest of the document as you go along but those references to the accused you deal with now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It sounds evidently sensible, and I can deal with that expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And speaking for myself, I'm not happy with the term "summary." If this document is to be admitted into evidence in one way or another, I think you will have to find another term for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour may remember that I made the point myself; this document happened to have been signed when we were only able to produce summaries. It was signed because the witness had been here and had then had to go away on account of the accused's ill health. And you never know when you may need a signed document, signed as to its truth. The witness may have to come back in the future. I entirely agree; from now on the word "summary" will not appear and it will be "statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has this witness ever given a prior statement apart from this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Given a prior statement indeed, and that's available should you wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, I think that this summary should give specific reference to the paragraphs in the -- of the prior statements, page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Generally, it would have done, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, for the preparation of the accused, for his defence or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's our almost invariable practice. Again, the problem here was we received at the last moment notice that because of the ill health of the accused it wasn't going to be possible for the evidence to be given. The summary had been prepared, and I think my recollection is that the witness only had time to go through it before flying away and we didn't get the annotations done. Normally they are done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will admit this document on the ground -- on the basis that -- of Rule 89(F), but counsel must summarise, the witness must summarise those -- the rest of the document and those parts which deal with the accused must be given live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will see what the position is about the document, but I think we need to have the practice clear that if an application is to be made under Rule 89(F), the Chamber must have the document before the hearing and -- and not on the same morning of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I'm only sorry that something went wrong somewhere, that you didn't have it at the beginning of the week or last week. May the witness come in and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- just a question of timing. We cannot sit beyond 1.45 today. We've got -- there's another case coming in to this court in the afternoon, in any event. Obviously this is an important witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And one who is very anxious about having had to have come back twice already. I'll just have to see how I can do, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The exhibits, I think, will come in with this witness in two or three different numberings, because as I've already explained, I'm going to deal with them as swiftly as I possibly can. And although I shan't be touching the extracts from Jovic's diary in any detail or at all, simply to draw to your attention that they're there, you'll find, I think, that they're highlighted as potentially relevant passages should the Chamber have any time to read them outside court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration, please. And would you stand to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, did you on your last visit to The Hague prepare, in cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor, a document called a summary but signed by you as to its truth and accuracy?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of qualifications or corrections identified yesterday; is that a document that is true?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be given an exhibit number. And for registry purposes, I can announce that there's no problem with distributing the document. Nothing will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 569, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have a copy in front of him in B/C/S to follow should he wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, by way of general summary, you were the last effective Prime Minister of the SFRY from the 16th of March of 1989 up until the 20th of December of 1991. And I think the position is you have avoided making any comment publicly on matters with which we are concerned since that date.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. After almost 12 years, this is the first time I'm speaking in public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your -- I'm going to call it a signed statement and a statement, because the word "summary" is inappropriate. Your statement sets out your background; your education as an electrical engineer, your long history in business and industry until you were persuaded in 1982 to enter politics, thereafter having roles as president of the executive council and president of the Presidency of the Republic of Croatia until you became the effective Prime Minister, by title president of the Federal Executive Council, on the 16th of March of 1989, being at all times a member of the Communist Party, still working as a businessman.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. When given authority to form a government, you were the first person to be able to make your own choice of office-holders, although in doing that, you consulted the republics. Of the various republics you consulted on a voluntary basis, which, if any, made demands for the position of favoured candidates?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The condition I put forward for accepting the authority to compose a government was to have the greatest possible freedom possible in such cases to form a government. I visited many institutions and had talks. I went to companies, to the various republics. And wherever I had talks - and this includes the highest bodies - no demands were placed upon me but everyone tried to meet my requests. It was only Mr. Milosevic who asked me for something quite definite. He wanted Serbia to have the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is touched upon in an annex of the -- or this topic is touched upon in an excerpt from Jovic's diary. The position, I think, Mr. Markovic, is that in preparation for giving evidence you have reviewed passages from that book that you had already read and that some of those passages are produced as exhibits for the Judges to consider if it's helpful. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I can say that I was at least a month late with my proposal for the government before the Federal Assembly because of Mr. Milosevic's request that at any cost he should have the post -- or rather, he should have control of the post of minister of the interior. I had my own candidate, Mr. Zemljaric, who was from Slovenia and who before that was the Prime Minister of Slovenia. Mr. Milosevic went so far as to insist, even after I offered him other solutions - I offered him the post of minister of foreign affairs for Serbia - but he rejected all this and insisted that Serbia should have the post of minister of the interior. He put forward various names, I rejected every one of them because in my opinion none of them was suitable. Finally, he proposed Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just deal with the administration of the exhibits. May the file of exhibits for this witness be given a number, presumably 57 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us just check these. These are virtually all and concern --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Many, but not all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- selections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are one or two others, some of which have already been tendered, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 570, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So 570 -- I simply alert Your Honours to 570, tab 1, is capable of covering or covers the same general topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gracanin thus became office-holder. Why was it, in your judgement, that the accused particularly wanted the Ministry of the Interior? Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear. Throughout this time, Milosevic persistently insisted on this, and in this way he showed what it was he wanted. He wanted to put under his control the intelligence services at all levels; although, in the development of Yugoslavia and its structures as a state, this was no longer such an important institution because every republic had its own Ministry of the Interior, which was well developed and they had their own intelligence and counterintelligence services. The army had this as well. In spite of this, at the federal level there was still many functions and a lot of information linked up to the post of minister of the interior, which were not negligible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man Gracanin eventually fell out of favour with Milosevic and we can see some reference to this - and I don't need you to expand on this - in tab 2 of the same exhibit, 570. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After we, as the federal government, developed our own conception and programme for reforms for democratisation of the country - and we were all working on this concept very correctly - there was no reason to exclude from this Gracanin and to have him function outside this team. And as he worked as part of this team, he accepted more and more the elements of this joint policy, those that pertained to his field of work. And, of course, having done this, he could no longer meet the demands made upon him by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For about a year and a half after forming your government, you had a stable and well-functioning government, the programme, paragraph 11, that introduced was one of economic reform and democratisation, you taking the view that the measures you took were not themselves reforms but were aimed at creating an environment where reform could happen. I think your programme included changes in politics, economy, society, and citizen rights, and it was a programme of several phases, starting with a stabilisation programme, moving through economic reforms towards privatisation, state reform, and a multi-party system. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. The first part of what you said, when you said it was not a real reform, it was a programme of stabilisation, to put a stop to inflation and to create the possibility of normal business and also all the other programmes which were to be implemented after this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your signed statement, at paragraph 11, by bullet points you identify what you were aiming at, and I needn't run through all of those. The accused's attitude in the Federal Assembly expressed through delegates from Serbia, Vojvodina, Kosovo, and Montenegro was what towards your programme?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: From the information I received from several deputies from Serbia, talks were held with the deputies, and they were given the task of toppling the programme put forward by the federal government. They said, "If we don't topple Ante Markovic now, we won't be able to do that in the next four years, and he is not favourable to us, so everything has to be done to topple him." However, at that session of the Federal Assembly, both bodies had a joint session, and I reported to them, putting forward all the basic elements of the programme, and I announced that the currency would become convertible and showed them the new convertible currency, which no one knew had been printed -- and that's a special story, how I managed to do this. At that moment, there was such thunderous applause, such ovations in the Assembly, that no one could put forward any objections. However, when bills were tabled in parliament, a sufficient number of deputies were found who did everything to try to impede this process of reforms to make it more difficult and to slow them down. In Serbia, for example, salaries were increased, and this was not supposed to be done in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it in the programme, in your judgement, in the programme that you were putting forward that was objectionable to the accused and his supporters?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, they had a global objection, saying that this programme would enrich the richer parts of the country and would further impoverish the poorer parts. Of course, a programme of reform for society is such that not every part of society is equally able to accept it and to implement it. Some need more time than others. And because there was a difference between the developed areas of Croatia and the underdeveloped areas of Croatia - Slovenia and Croatia were more developed; Serbia was in the middle; Macedonia, Bosnia, and Herzegovina were less developed than the average - and because of this, the government made a decision within the scope of the programme that the foreign obligations of Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Kosovo would be taken over by the government. This, as far as I can recall -- it's been quite a long time, but it amounted to, I think, 988 billion dollars. This was not an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. inconsiderable amount, which was transferred from the budgets of the republics to the level of the Federation, which was to pay all this. There were some other elements where they were favoured.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Do I need to expand further? There were other objections as well. One of these was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just if I could interrupt you for one minute, Mr. Markovic. You realise that time is a problem, and I know that your concerns about coming back, so there's a balance between the fullest answer and getting things done in a summary way. If I can move you on just at this extent: What, in your judgement, if any, was the accused's personal objection to your programme? Which of his personal objectives was thwarted by it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There are several elements here that we could discuss, but I'm afraid it would take too long, so I'll try to be very rational with time. Number one, the implementation of the reforms of the state, the state system, then the legal system because ultimately Mr. Milosevic used the street to topple his political opponents. He used a kind of political lynching, and he would no longer be able to do this if democracy developed. Further, he was to be put on an equal footing with all the others, and he could not usurp the rights he was usurping, because such communication would be established between society, the parliaments, the governments, and all the political elements, because when a reform is implemented, not only an economic but also a political and social reform and society is democratised and the state is reformed and all this was part of the programme in its entirety, then rights could no longer be usurped by one man, who although he had no legal basis was able to control everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned how --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should say, Your Honours, that through the witness the approach to the witness's democratisation programme and other aspects of the programme of the accused and of Jovic is dealt with in tab 3 of Exhibit 570, or touched on at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned how salaries were raised. Can you tell us, please, what was or approximately what was the level of inflation when you took over the reins of government?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was several thousand a year, the level of growth. And after the programme, regardless of the fact that because of the demands of the Serbian delegation, talks were prolonged and certain elements were implemented with delays, 10- or 15-day delays, the programme could not be implemented on the same day and this was one of the prerequisites for its success. But by April inflation had been reduced to zero, and in May and June I think it was even below zero, and this was the first time in any socialist country that inflation had been reduced to zero. Besides this, we managed to establish large hard currency reserves. According to the French governor of the central bank, we had larger hard currency reserves than many European countries, and they amounted to almost 11 billion dollars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, against your programme of economic reform, you've mentioned how salaries were raised. I think was there also a one-and-a-half-hour strike staged in Belgrade on the 20th of December of 1989? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was organised, and about 600.000 people took part, protesting against the programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the accused express his views - just yes or no - about the programmes reforms in closed sessions of the Serbian Assembly and the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact. I know that the Serb government, which met during those days, did give a negative response to the reform, and it also gave a negative answer, and so did the government of Vojvodina. They gave a negative answer, and the government of Montenegro had certain remarks and criticisms to make, which is logical, but in general terms this attitude meant that it was being rejected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have explained how on producing as a surprise, and I think actually waiving the currency, you were able to attract wide support. Was the position - paragraph 15 - that by the beginning of 1990 opinion polls put your popularity higher than Kucan's in Slovenia and indeed higher than the accused's in Serbia, so that had you been able to have elections at that time you would have been almost inevitably somebody who couldn't be defeated?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right. All the opinion polls at the time spoke highly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: -- of myself. They assessed me highly. And this, of course, emerged from the overall programme, a comprehensive programme which had never been put forward in Yugoslavia until then. And the conditions were ripe for it, and of course this was one of the reasons for which certain people felt envy, and they felt they could be politically jeopardised. Within the frameworks of the programme put forward by my government were necessary changes to be made, new laws to be drafted, and the constitution too for general Yugoslav elections to be held, and we wanted to go to the polls generally, for a general Yugoslav election straight away, but certain points in the constitution had to be changed and the representatives of the two republics came out emphatically against that, that is to say, of Serbia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to summarise a few matters from your statement. And I hope if I get them right, you'll be able to acknowledge that by a simple yes or no. You've told us about reducing inflation to zero, paragraph 16, and having foreign currency reserves I think of the order of 11 billion dollars and getting a positive balance of payments. And you also had some 65.000 private companies established during your very first year in office. All correct? Just yes if it is.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. And we could even say that this was in -- within the space of a year and a half, because in the first nine months, from the 16th of March, 1989, until the 18th of December, when I came out with the programme, that same year, that is, I was diligent in preparing the programme and devised the preconditions for putting it into practice. And when it started to be implemented, then those were the results that were scored. And let me also add that the country's debts at that time dropped from 21 and a half billion dollars to 12.2 billion dollars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph -- thank you. Paragraph 18. One of the problems - and we've heard about this from another witness - was the primary issue of money, that is, the printing of money. You would not support subsidies to the agricultural sector by the primary issue of money, planning for agriculture to be supported from elsewhere and achieving a regime where agricultural product prices did not rise, indeed where you had stockpiles of wheat, corn, and other -- other commodities to intervene in order to control prices. As part of your anti-inflation approach, you ended a policy whereby goods exported to the USSR were paid automatically by the bank without proof of receipt of the money from the USSR, and this, I think, is one of the various things commented on by Jovic in his book, you trying to stop that practice, you seeking to have proof of payment to the Yugoslav National Bank before providers could themselves be paid. And this, again, led to an improvement in the exchange rate for clearinghouse of the dollar. And this is all covered, the first parts, I think, at tab 4, and the second passage is at tab 5 of Exhibit 570 in Jovic's book. Just yes or no, if I've summarised the position correctly, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've summarised it very correctly. May I just add the following: It was customary in Yugoslavia before our government, and especially before this particular programme, to make great use of primary emissions for the financing of different areas and for financing the budget deficit, also to finance agriculture and the deficit that was incurred with the exchanges with the Soviet Union. Our firm decision as a component part of our programme was that we must not use primary emission, even to finance the budget of the Federation, except in extraordinary cases, which were stipulated. So when it came to agriculture, we provided resources to assist agriculture within the budget, and we allocated these resources through the budget and not by printing money from the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Now, as far as the Soviet Union is concerned, we had an enormous debt run up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An eye to the time, Mr. Markovic, a matter for you, but it's really -- you may think -- if we can just deal with it in summary, it's satisfactory. Just to get the context right, of course, the 1989 budget was the budget that applied to the calendar year 1990. And then at the end of 1990, you prepared a budget for the calendar year 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to the difficulties that you encountered in that second budgetary year - paragraph 20 of the signed statement - was there an incident involving the accused which you describe as "the robbery of the century"? Please just explain it to us in a couple of sentences and your contacts with the accused about it.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1990, I received information from my friends that the Serbian government or Serbian National Bank had made a break-through, had broken into the monetary system, and that it had transferred to the Central Bank of Serbia, the National Bank of Serbia, 18.2 billion dinars for its purposes without any coverage. That was daylight robbery, pure and simple. And it shook the very foundations of Yugoslavia. Mr. Milosevic, who bragged a lot and said he was fighting for Yugoslavia, showed how much this was true and how much he was actually fighting for his own interests. When I received that information, I called him up straight away. I got him over the phone, and I talked to him, and I was very sharp with him. Mr. Milosevic said he knew nothing about it, and I told him that there was not a single detail that was going on in Serbia which could have gone on without his knowledge and without him agreeing to it, let alone this kind of daylight robbery, to the tune of 2 and a half billion German marks. All he said was that he would look into the matter. And I said, "There's nothing to look into. What you must do is take steps immediately and rescind that decision and put the money back." He said he would investigate the matter, and if that were true that that was what he would do. He didn't, of course, do that, but I convened a government meeting straight away and the government ordered the National Bank -- the Central Bank of Yugoslavia to take the most rigorous steps vis-a-vis the National Bank of Serbia and to have the moneys sent back as urgently as possible. And I think that indeed in the space of two or three weeks the money was returned. About 10 billion, I would say, approximately. However, the rest of the money was never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that 1 billion approximate Deutschmarks shifted from the federal --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes, 1 -- actually, 2 and a half billion marks were returned but 1 and a half billion we never got back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the robbery had been achieved by manipulation of the banking system; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, through a manipulation of the banking system. It wasn't real money, it was quasi-money, the kind of transactions that banks have amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, Jovic's account of this can be found at tab 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we move on to the next year, the budgetary difficulties of 1991. By this time - paragraph 21 - were difficulties arising because Slovenia and Croatia were retaining taxes they would otherwise have paid to the federal budget, and this made balancing the books that much more difficult?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At first, when the budget was established for 1991, we still had normal conditions prevailing, regardless of what the National Bank of Serbia had done by breaking into the system of the National Banks of Yugoslavia. And we set up the budget in the same way we had set it up in 1990 and 1989 -- or rather, the 1989-1990 fiscal year. However, within the -- within that year, there was greater tension in relations between individual parts of Yugoslavia, especially Slovenia and Croatia and Serbia, or that portion which was under Milosevic's control, which wasn't only Serbia. And then at one stage, when they proclaimed their independence and secession, that is to say, Slovenia and Croatia, what happened was that they usurped the funds which were direct resources from the budget of the Federation, such as customs, taxation, revenues and so on. And in that way, in actual fact, the budget was left without a large portion of the federal resources, federal funds. And Serbia took the decision not to pay into the budget any more, so for a time it was only Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia, which were in fact the poorest regions or amongst the poorest regions at that period of time, and they were not able to cover the needs and requirements stemming from the responsibilities that the budget had to tend to. And so there were calls for emissions of money, financing by this method, but we can only do that up to a certain level, because the regulations did not allow us to do that and to become indebted in that way. However, as major changes had taken place in the second half of 1991 and as there were major changes in the National Bank as well, because the governors had stepped down from the Council of the National Bank of Yugoslavia, the governors of Croatia and Slovenia, in fact, they had stepped down, so that it was impossible to keep emission and the printing of money under control, because it was the governors' council who would okay that. And then what happened was what Mr. Milosevic did when he took over 18.2 billion, billions. This was primary emission. Money was emitted, printed, and the insistence was that those moneys should be used to finance various areas. I was not able to prevent any of that, so that I was -- became impotent in various areas and in that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And indeed by the autumn and early winter of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the autumn and early winter of 1991, you found yourself isolated and alone in government - paragraph 22 of this signed statement - with no support and no chance of taking matters forward. And there came a time when you produced a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not intending that we should take the witness through this in detail now. He provided it to us yesterday. We've managed to get a draft translation. It's a document of several sides, but it summarises events. And I would ask that that may be added to the Exhibit 569 and perhaps become -- 570, I beg your pardon, and perhaps become its tab 16, if that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that you prepared this report, Mr. Markovic? We're not going to go through it at the moment, but it's available for the Judges to read.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will, however, ask you to do something with a rather shorter document, which is to read at this stage the statement you made when you finally resigned from office on the 20th of December before you left for Graz via Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I wonder if this statement could become tab 17. Again, it's the subject of a draft translation and a final translation will have to be provided in due course.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: "Thank you very much for giving me the opportunity of publishing the statement in its entirety of the president of the Federal Executive Council who has tendered his resignation. Allow me to read it out. It is very brief: The political crisis and the war have eliminated the results of the reform and the process of democratisation. Neither the support of the world or the European Community or the United Nations or the United States of America, the Troika, the 14 agreements on a cease-fire from Igalo to Geneva, The Hague Conference, were not able to make for a peaceful solution of the Yugoslav crisis but the flames of war broke out more and more, with thousands of casualties, destroyed towns and villages in Croatia. There's the threat to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the enormous number of refugees, mostly poor people who have been left without anything. The economic catastrophe is therefore becoming deeper with the growth of hyper-inflation, millions of people unemployed, the production reductions, a great deal of poverty for millions of people, the citizens of this country who are not to blame for any of this and which will necessarily lead to a social explosion of unprecedented proportions. For anything to be done to stop this imminent process of disintegration, each individual and all of us together must do everything to stop the war, to establish peace, and to enable the arrival of the Blue Helmets. And on the basis of general European principles and documents that have already been adopted, including The Hague one and the Brussels one, to seek to find a solution to the Yugoslav crisis through peaceful means and agreement. The Federal Executive Council in that process of stopping economic and social crises, as well as war devastation, has been made completely incapable of doing so. It has no competence or authority, nor is it allowed to work, let alone to wage any sort of policy with the budget for the following year, which from the Federal Executive Council is being required, should be financed and politically supported, because about 81 per cent of the budget goes towards financing the Yugoslav People's Army, which is quite outside the control of the Federal Executive Council. The revenue for this is found through emissions, which means the printing of money, and this contributes to the growth of hyper-inflation. This means not only a continuation of war and death and destruction but the loss of all economic and social prospects, and I always during my term of office fought to counteract this. So I see no other possibility than to resign because I was always for democracy and peace and against war, and that is why a war budget for me is quite unacceptable and I cannot put anything like that forward and shall not do so. As the Assembly at the SFRY is no longer functioning as a parliament able to represent all sections of Yugoslavia and as the Rump Presidency is not qualified to bring in valid decisions, there is no organ or institution which would legally be able to give me back my term of office, and in that respect I am ready to involve myself in all activities that will be required of me by the lawful representatives of the country in order to prevent war, mutual killing, and in the quest for a peaceful and democratic solution to the crisis. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then having read that resignation statement, telling journalists about your decision, you flew to Graz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to come back to paragraphs 23 to 50 at the end and deal with them as succinctly as I can. But may we now turn to paragraph 51.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, having set the overall political scene in which you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. encountered the accused, can we deal in a little more detail with your personal contacts with him. First seeing him, I think, in Zagreb in about 1986 or 1987, in relation to a man Ivan Stambolic, of whom we've heard and who was a friend of yours. Did he organise a visit of Serbian officials to Croatia and was that the first time when you met the accused?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, your first working contact with him concerned Stambolic. In summary, can you explain what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: One day, after a session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia at which Milosevic toppled Ivan Stambolic and threw him out of the Central Committee, as well as a number of other people who were together there with Stambolic, he called me up. At that time, I was president of the Presidency of Croatia. But for many years I was also one of the leading people in the Yugoslav Bank for Economic Cooperation. And as the director and president of Rade Koncar, which was one of Yugoslavia's largest companies, which I led for 24 years, I insisted greatly on organising businessmen to set up the JUBMES Bank for economic support to exports from Yugoslavia, and this proved to be an excellent idea. Milosevic asked me whether I could find a place for Ivan Stambolic in that bank, the Bank for International Economic Cooperation. As I had a high regard for Ivan Stambolic and as I knew that his survival in Serbia would be, to say the least, bitter or practically impossible, I accepted to do this and I helped him come to the post of president of that bank. At the time, Ilija Marijanovic was the bank's president - he's another good friend of mine - and we met and we discussed this matter, and we discussed his tendering his resignation so that the road be open for Ivan Stambolic, and that's how Ivan Stambolic came to be elected general director of JUBMES and Ilija Marijanovic remained as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that business encounter with the accused, you then found yourself having the mandate of forming the government. Was your appointment something of which he ever appeared to approve?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference between courtesy and doing something just in informal terms and in actual substance. Of course, he would congratulate people, but of course everything that was done from the first day was done and geared towards making it impossible for the government to function at whose head I stood. On many occasions, relations were severed, and we could mention an instance in point; with respect to the re-election of Stambolic to the post of president of the Yugoslav Bank for reconstruction and development, for example, which is when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Which is when Milosevic asked me that the Federal Executive Council should not lend its support to the re-election of Stambolic. In fact, that bank was a bank of a large number of Yugoslav companies, export companies. But also, the federal state had its own interests there, and via the budget it had participation in the proprietary of the bank, but it didn't have the majority vote, and the state always wields great influence in that respect. So he asked me to propose on behalf of the Federal Executive Council that Stambolic should not be re-elected as bank president. I refused to do that. There was no reason for that, and in fact Milosevic made it be known that he personally did not like to have Stambolic around and that he was interfering in certain affairs in Serbia, which, as he said, wasn't a good thing either for Stambolic or for Serbia, as he put it. I didn't know about all this, and I don't think it could have been proved either. So I refused to do that, and Milosevic then proceeded to write a letter, addressing it to the Federal Executive Council, officially asking the Federal Executive Council of the Yugoslav government not to support Stambolic's election. And I, of course, informed the Federal Executive Council about this and asked them to authorise me to function along those lines. I was given the power to do so, and I went to the bank Assembly meeting and lent my support to the re-election of Stambolic, who won the vast majority of votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this time --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Many companies from Serbia even voted for him. And may I just finish, please. After that, Milosevic cut off all communications with me and the federal government for the next few months, which means that for him it wasn't important that a state system should be allowed to function. And Serbia was the largest republic in Yugoslavia. He didn't like his demands being rejected. And because of that, he blocked work between Serbia and the federal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One point, not quite clear from what you said: At this time, was Stambolic also a potential political competitor of the accused?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In formal terms, he was not. And he did his best not to meddle in politics at all. However, by the positions he took, not only in Serbia but in Yugoslavia as well, Stambolic was a highly-respected man. He was a very diligent and honest man. And by his very existence, he presented a danger to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to paragraph 53 for some general points. When dealing with the accused, was he straightforward and open in his manner of dealing? And a second point: We've heard some evidence that he dealt with people on a one-to-one basis. What was your experience?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it differed. Milosevic very rarely said what he thought, and also he hardly ever did what he thought, so that it was very difficult to assess all this. You would have to take everything with a pinch of salt, some reservations, and look at the global trends and then deduce why he was doing something. So I never gained the impression that he did something along those lines, something that would be constructive for the whole country. I was not able to deduce that from anything, and I also have to say that never in front of me did he speak of a Greater Serbia. He always came out in favour of Yugoslavia. However, at the same time what he was doing was undermining Yugoslavia, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, why didn't Mr. Milosevic get his way in having Stambolic removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did not depend on him, so he was not able to do this, because the Yugoslav Bank for Economic Cooperation was an institution at the Yugoslav level. It did not fall within his competence. It was quite independent. And if anyone was competent over it, it was the federal government. So he was unable to exert any influence on the replacement of Ivan Stambolic, apart from persuading some members of the Assembly of the Yugoslav Bank to vote against him at the annual Assembly. But as I said before, the majority of delegates in the Assembly of JUBMES, this bank, voted in favour of Stambolic, not against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The -- I'll just get the tab reference. The tab reference to what we've been dealing with is -- well, I'll find it in a second and come back to that. Is it 8? Sorry. I'll come back to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as the other things that he did following his unsuccessful attempt to remove Stambolic, were you attacked in the press by him and also by Jovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only Jovic. In this period of time, after I refused to support Milosevic's demand that Stambolic be replaced, there was a media campaign in Serbia and beyond. I think there was something in Montenegro as well -- against me. It was organised against me personally and not the Federal Executive Council. And there is something I would like to add. I don't know to what extent it's relevant, but when the NATO attack on Serbia occurred because of Kosovo, Ivan Stambolic contacted me. He was in Bulgaria at the time. And, of course, the two of us had socialised quite a lot while I was in Belgrade, and we had the same opinions and world view, so we became very close and were able to talk rather intimately. He told me when he called me from Bulgaria, "Ante, I can see how things are developing. Although I have refused to do so up to now, I will have to become politically active." And I, of course, supported this. I felt that the time was coming when Serbia would need him. It seems that someone else understood this besides myself, which is why Stambolic disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us make sure that we have for the record the right tab number for Stambolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 14 was the -- I'm sorry not to have been it at my fingertips. Tab 14 was the one that dealt with the previous passage, and we're just moving on now to tab 15, which is paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the fall of 1990, Mr. Markovic, did the accused approach you in respect of a constitutional change and did he make a proposal to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This was when, let's say, an unofficial chat about this and that, when we were advocating constitutional reforms, at one point Milosevic said: "It would be best to go for changes of the constitution that would remove the Presidency, which is ineffective and which is in fact impeding work in this country, and that instead of the Presidency there should be a president. I propose, if you agree, that we both work on this, and we are prepared to nominate you for president," I waved this aside; I didn't take it seriously. In order to carry out amendments to the constitution, you needed the approval of all republics, and it was a very complicated and long process, which could not be realised that quickly. But I wasn't at all interested in that. If that's what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is touched on to the degree it is at tab 15. And can I now move to Karadjordjevo and the March 1991 meeting between Tudjman and the accused. Following that meeting, did you have meetings with both Tudjman and the accused where they spoke of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are two ways of dealing with this: You can either, as it's set out in your statement, deal with the way in which their accounts to you had elements in common; or, whichever is most convenient for you, you can tell us item by item -- not item by item -- person by person what the accused and what Tudjman said to you. Can you give us an account of what you were told.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As I had received information about the topic discussed in Karadjordjevo, that is, the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina between Serbia and Croatia, and that Milosevic and Tudjman had agreed to carry out this division, and also there was talk of the dismissal of the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, because he was in the way of both of them in implementing this division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At my initiative, I had a meeting with Milosevic in Belgrade and with Tudjman in Zagreb. According to my custom, I spoke to both of them very openly. The results of these talks were that both of them confirmed to me that they had agreed to divide up Bosnia and Herzegovina. Milosevic told me this very soon. Tudjman needed much more time to admit this and to say that they had reached an understanding about it. They did not have identical interpretations of this agreement. Milosevic said that Bosnia and Herzegovina was an artificial entity created by Tito, that it could not survive, and that most of the Muslims were in fact Orthodox who had been forced to change their religion. When I asked him directly or, rather, I asked both of them directly, "Do you think --" that's what I said to Milosevic, "Do you think that this will be so simple? Do you think you will be able to do this without bloodshed, without blood up to the knees?" Milosevic said he didn't believe that. He said that Bosnia and Herzegovina anyway has a majority of Serbs and Croats in the population so that there would be no conflict, and that they had envisioned an enclave for the Muslims, the two of them, and that the Muslims could live in that enclave. I asked the same question of Tudjman. I said to him, among other things, "Do you think that people who will be born and who will die to the sound of gunfire, that this will not transform Bosnia and Herzegovina into a kind of Palestine? How many victims will there be? How much destruction? How much will be ruined?" Tudjman thought this would not be the way things would happen. He said, "Europe will not allow a Muslim state in its heart. We will gain the support of European. And as for your fears that there will be war there, all I can say is Bosnia fell silently," because in history Bosnia once fell without an armed struggle, so there is this saying in our language that Bosnia fell with a whisper. Tudjman said that the Muslims were anyway Catholics who had been forced to adopt Islam. So each of these men admitted and thought this was something quite normal. Tudjman even asked for my approval and support that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be divided. With respect to the dismissal of the federal Prime Minister, both of them said this was true but each of them said that this had been proposed by the other. But, of course, the other had no reason to disagree. In any case, I parted with both of them totally dissatisfied and said I would fight against this to the end and that I would do whatever was in my power - and this was not much, but there was still something I could do - to prevent such an intervention in Bosnia and Herzegovina which could not but end in bloodshed, refugees, ethnic cleansing, and a destroyed economy and society. And this is precisely what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps, without inconveniencing the Chamber too much, we can go back, for chronological reasons, to paragraph 35, to give some sequencing of events. Mr. Markovic, in July of 1991 -- no, I beg your pardon. There's something I've forgotten. Can you just tell us, in respect of your meeting with the accused about Karadjordjevo -- at Karadjordjevo, how did the accused end his explanation of what -- of what had happened? What did he say as to his forecast for the future, arising from what had happened at Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He told me what I've just said, that nothing would happen, that this would succeed because of the ratio of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. And when I insisted and said, "What if war does break out?" he said, "Well, then we'll see what we'll do," and he didn't go into it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate to either or both of these men whether you would accept what they'd done or whether you would contest it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I have just said that I told them I would contest it with all means at my disposal, which were not very large but by any means I had at my disposal I would fight against this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform Izetbegovic -- the late Izetbegovic about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not right away; a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to -- in your signed statement, to paragraph 35. From your relationship with Izetbegovic in July 1991, were you informed of a plan to arm the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I visited Macedonia and Kiro Gligorov and Alija Izetbegovic in Bosnia often. There was not a month where I didn't go to see them, exchange views with them, exchange information, and thus Izetbegovic informed me that they had intercepts of conversations between Milosevic and Karadzic from which it was evident that Serbian paramilitary units in Bosnia and Herzegovina were being armed. I asked him to give me these intercepts, and he sent them to me by his minister of the interior, who came to see me in Belgrade and who played the tapes for me. There were several tapes. And from these, I recognised Milosevic's voice and Karadzic's voice. They were discussing the organisation of armies, the arrival of helicopters, the arrival of a colonel, an RAM programme which I was not aware of, I don't know what it was, and of ammunitions which were to be taken from certain places and sent to certain places. Alija Delimustafic, the minister, showed me this. When I asked him to give me this because there was a session of the Federal Executive Council taking place, I wanted to play this there, but he disagreed and he deleted the tapes. I gave this information to the cabinet, but in any case this is the information I received. I told the government meeting about it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry on. Sorry. The government, having been told about it, what --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Admiral Brovet was there at the session, and he denied this. He said it was impossible, he said this was a forgery, that the army had nothing to do with this. But this was absolutely untrue, because I clearly recognised the voices, and it was quite clear that they were discussing the handover of weapons and the places where weapons could be acquired. I heard a tape like this here in your office, and I didn't hear the ones that Delimustafic played for me, but I did hear similar ones here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: -- where RAM is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was one tape that you listened to. It's tab 30 -- Exhibit 353, tab 31. It's been played already. It's available for listening to again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see the time. I'm in the Chamber's hands as to whether it should be done now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time for the adjournment now. Mr. Markovic, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you remember, as we tell all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include speaking to the members of the Prosecution about it. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered the position, Mr. Nice, about the extracts from the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And our practice, which we adopted with the last witness, we propose to adopt with this one, which is at this stage to mark the extracts for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they will be marked in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Two tiny administrative points: The late provision to Your Honours of the summary now referred to as a statement of the witness was not something in respect of which I was making any complaint or -- on whom I was allocating any responsibility. I always assume I am to blame for anything until anyone tells me otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With -- I don't know that you were to blame, but there was plainly some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a misunderstanding. Is a reflection a rather good thing. The separation of powers between Bench and bar is overcome to the extent it can by the telephone system. And as the Chamber knows, the telephone system has been in a only partially work-operative form this week and we've all been unable to get in touch with the other. In any case, I think the misunderstanding has been sorted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out. And the second thing is that I do now have, courtesy of Ms. Bauer, an annotated version of the statement identifying from which paragraphs of the original witness statement various items have been drawn. So if anybody wants the references, I have them to hand. We're at the moment in paragraph 35 of the statement, and I'd like the witness now to hear part of an already-produced transcript, which Your Honours may recall, part of Exhibit 353, tab 31. It's on Sanction, and we're going to pick it up where the accused picks up the open line and just take it a little bit on beyond that, but not very far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Radovan, I spoke to the highest place. Good. Please, you need to understand this, because as they say, I don't have -- I cannot explain everything. All right. It is of strategic importance for the future RAM. You know what RAM is? Yes, I know. I know everything. That the Banja Luka group is ready and mobile. All right. This is why you must, first, make sure that it is able and mobile and that it has no problems. And secondly, call Uzelac in one hour and invite him to an agreement. All right. At the highest level. All right. All the additional people that you can provide. Yes. That they need to stay and keep their houses and the territory and block those centres of the HDZ, et cetera. They shall be armed. And they shall be provided with everything, we shall fly the helicopters in and all that ... Excellent. I also ask you to -- Accordingly, I ask you personally regulate numbers one and two. All these other matters, Kupres, this is very important. Good. And the third thing I told you, the rally, it is very important because of the international community. Yes, that's underway. But, tell me, can we arrange the same thing, that they give me back the armament of the TO in Sipovo and Mrkonjic. That's a small matter. All right. Let them arm them there, here I -- we've got 170 ready in Mrkonjic and 150 in Sipovo and they're ready to go to Kupres. Is Uzelac also in charge of that? No, no, that is -- I think that is him, yes, yes. Tell him that, brother, no problems. We cannot discuss every small detail like this. All right. All right. These 150 and 170 shall go to Kupres and there we've got 750 people. Yes. It is also important for us that this battalion, which is mobilised by the army is in Kupres and that everything be as it should be. It shall be, but if they receive this. Those who stay should put themselves under their command because Kupres is terribly -- that's 50/50 and the Serbs suffered horribly there during the war. Let me tell you something, even this crazy Seselj fucked the opposition yesterday. I saw, I heard. You know what he told hem he said, "Did you decide to attack the JNA now when the JNA needs to defend the Serb people." Yes, yes, that's. That's the one he says has the tie of Zimmerman's waiter on. Yes, yes. Fucking hell. Yes, yes. It is even clear to him. Clear, clear, certainly And it is not clear to they'd those traitors. I saw it, I saw. Yesterday in direct contact with Mesic. Have you got a number of Uzelac by any chance? I don't, but you shall find it. Let these find it for you. Yes, yes, all right. Let them find it for you, and please, in an hour. All right. It is now one o'clock. Call him at two. All right. And please tell him that I wish to secure a maximal political support ... Is he going to accept more of our boys if he needs them, or just the ones that already ... He shall receive them if needed. But you give him as many as you judge that should stay there. Everything shall be transported for them in the helicopters, so they've got everything. So that they stay and guard. All right, agreed. Accordingly, you've got everything. Agreed. But now it is to be or not to be concerning Krajina because they wish to cut off Krajina. Yes, yes. They don't want to go to Knin because many of them would get killed, but they do want to come from behind. Yes, yes. Now we shall ... ... in the JNA, that shan't stop them there. How is it going to stop them with the armour alone, if there's no brigade? All right, agreed. Everything will be all right. When, I mean, now is, as they say, war and this is one of the sides. There are no problems whatsoever. Please take care of it. Only if these numbers work, I think it shall be completed. Everything must work. I will, I will, all right. Talk to you, do call again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the tape of an intercept you heard when in The Hague a few weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two voices on the tape, can you recognise either of both of them?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Both of them, very distinctly. It was Milosevic and Karadzic talking. This is the same tape that Delimustafic brought to me in Belgrade and that I heard there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's one of a series of tapes that covered the topics you spoke about before we adjourned half an hour ago?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do these tapes in general reveal to you that what was happening in the territory of which you were Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Very clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening? Just remind us. I know we've covered it, but just remind us, what was happening on the territory?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's very clear: These were preparations for war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were discussing the deployment of the army, the arming of men, the procurement of weapons, Banja Luka, and so on. It's quite clear. Helicopters and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lest anybody is interested in the detail and you can help us with the explanation, the reference to the one with the tie of Zimmerman's waiter, can you remember who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that, but I have no idea who it refers to. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This transcript has been produced, I think, earlier for identification, marked for identification. I don't necessarily invite a change in the status of that by reason of this evidence, but this is evidence that says this transcript existed in July of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we in the statement return, please, to paragraph 59, on page 20, paragraph 16 of the witness's original statement for anybody following that. Were you in The Hague, Mr. Markovic, in October or November of 1991 with presidents of the republic when Vukovar and Dubrovnik were being shelled or had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have short conversations with both the accused and Tudjman about this?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain. First I talked to Milosevic and asked him whether he could see what was happening in Vukovar and Dubrovnik. I asked him how he could allow Dubrovnik to be shelled, a famous place like that, important for the culture of this country and for world culture. Milosevic replied, "Who would be crazy enough to shell Dubrovnik? Dubrovnik isn't being shelled." But it was clear, you could see on television that it was being shelled. I then asked Milosevic to go and see Tudjman, wanting Tudjman to confirm to Milosevic that what I was saying was true and that Dubrovnik was being shelled. I repeated my statement. He replied in the same way, saying that this was impossible, that it couldn't be because were this the case, he would know about it. And Tudjman replied to this quite calmly, "Well, you see what Milosevic says." He didn't say anything in favour of an intervention against the shelling of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The inference that you drew from this as a politician on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it imposed itself logically. The conclusion was that Milosevic did wield influence, quite obviously, on what was happening, and Tudjman didn't find it to be in his interest that Dubrovnik should not be shelled, and Vukovar either, or rather, it suited him in the sense of winning over arguments for his emancipation or for his secession and having Croatia recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that last conversation, the conversation where Tudjman said you'd heard what the accused had said, who else was present, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Sarinic was. He was the chief of Tudjman's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing generally with the accused's ability to control events at this time and to deal with the army, is there something you want to say about the agreement at Igalo not covered in the signed statement? But you can rest assured the Chamber has heard of the Igalo agreement before.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear. Three men - Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic - signed the agreement in Igalo, and later on it was to be transformed into other agreements right up until Geneva, and I think it's quite clear; three men that held political power, that had weapons in their hands, and that had in one way or another their soldiers, who were able to obey them or not obey them, they signed the agreement and thus took responsibility upon themselves for the weapons and for everything that was to follow. They didn't stop it, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last meeting with the accused, dealt with at paragraph 60 of your latest statement, paragraph 32 of the original, longer version, was in Belgrade. And although you haven't dealt with this, I could perhaps summarise it to you. In your last few weeks or months in Belgrade, were things becoming potentially dangerous for you? Did you respond to that danger not by surrounding yourself with bodyguards and close protection but by doing no more than sleeping with a pistol under your pillow at night?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: For me, those last months were not -- it's not enough to say difficult; they were highly risky. I had a driver who came from Zagreb with me and who drove me while I was working for the Rade Koncar company and in the Croatian institutions, he was my chauffeur there. And I had a man from the security service whom I could rely upon 100 per cent. All the rest I eliminated. I didn't ask anybody to safeguard me. In the situation that I was in, the greatest danger could have come from the people actually providing security for me. And in history, that has been proved right many times, that those who allegedly are there to keep someone safe end up by killing them. Of course, symbolically speaking, I slept more peacefully by having my own pistol and keeping it under the pillow; although, that was just a gesture, because what could I do if I was faced with people who were well armed and so on and wanted to eliminate me? However, my talk with Mr. Milosevic took place sometime at the beginning of December, that is to say, just three or four weeks before I left Belgrade. And the main -- or rather, I asked for the meeting, and the meeting was held in Mr. Milosevic's cabinet. We were alone, there was nobody else there, and we mostly analysed the situation. I said I had come to analyse the situation, in fact, which was a terrible one, and which had its ramifications. The crisis was being made more difficult, there was no chance of an agreement being reached, we were faced with imminent war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Mr. Milosevic to that said, "What war? Which war?" And I think that was his customary sort of turn of phrase, regardless of the fact that I knew about it. I had listened to the conversation sometime in the middle of that same year, the conversation Mr. Milosevic had with Karadzic, and it was quite obvious that they were arming and preparing themselves, and he said, "Which war? There's no war, nor will there be a war." Anyway, that conversation, as far as I was concerned, was time-out, if I can put it that way, and I would leave the conviction that I would continue to work in the Federal Executive Council, regardless of having made my decision to leave, and, on the other hand, to try and gain an impression of future plans, Mr. Milosevic's future plans, although he never stated them clearly, but I was able to draw my own conclusions from what he said. And the conversation took the following -- those kinds of lines. And that was all, no other characteristic features.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any allegation to the accused by -- about what he'd done and what effect he'd had on your political decisions and movement?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't have a conversation along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all your conversations with the accused - and I think I've probably come to the end of questions about that topic - were you able to discern whether he was a Serb nationalist, in your judgement?, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Slobodan Milosevic used everything he could to ensure power for himself and power over people. And if that was nationalism, well, then he used nationalism. But in principle, he wasn't a nationalist. He was quite simply somebody who was ready to use everything at his disposal to secure power for himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we return, then, to earlier parts of the statement, which I'll take more briefly, having dealt with the overall history and the involvement of the accused in direct conversations, although he features in other bits of the evidence. Paragraph 23. Mr. Markovic, I intend to summarise lots of these passages, if I can, and where it's possible simply to say that I've got it right by saying yes, that may save time. Paragraph 23. The military budget was part of the general budget initially prepared by the Ministry of Defence and adjusted. The Presidency would be informed about it and the Federal Assembly would take the final decision on it, so that in preparations for the 1991 budget that took place in 1990, the government and you still had control. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 24 deals with the authority required for the primary emission of money. And I think you've dealt with a large part of that already, including the fact that Milosevic had no influence on decisions of the Council of Governors in 1989 and 1990, although this did change in the second half of 1991. For what reason, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the change from these sources of financing to finance the budget and the army, because contributions were not being paid in nor were taxes being paid or customs dues either. And on the other hand, in the years that led up to that time, it was legally made impossible for the National Bank to print money, unless it had certain reserves and grounds for doing so. But -- also, the Council of Governors and its members, who would have to have okayed the primary emission was such that the governor of each republic and autonomous province was a member of the Governor's Council. And already at that time, in the middle of the year, there was nobody from the National Bank of Slovenia or Croatia, so that was -- its positions were weakened, if I can put it that way, the position of the Council of Governors, because Milosevic had complete domination of it and could make the decisions he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours may want to note that at the end of paragraph 24, on page 9, the second-to-last line should be corrected. Where it says "the republics have left the council," should read "because the governors of the national banks of the Republics of Croatia and Slovenia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't need to take you through the exhibits already produced by Morten Torkildsen. The Jovic book reference is tab 7, and we can move on to some other miscellaneous topics. Very briefly, please: The public auditing service, or the SDK, was that the only tool available for carrying out financial transactions between institutions in the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, money transactions, financial transactions went through the public auditing service, the SDK. There was no other way of communication. And we had already prepared a reform which would move this competency to the banks, but that was not done at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that it remained possible to move money to the regions outside Serbia --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
