utterances.text: Yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- at a time when, if they were in some independent state, they should have been raising their own taxes or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They could have, but they didn't have the necessary organisation nor were capable of actually doing so. They didn't have any great money transactions. So it was logical to expect that part of the financing for such independent islands within a whole was to be financed from outside, and the only way was for them to go via the public auditing service and its channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 26. Your experience of the Serbian government and the Presidency showed you what as to the accused's control over the government Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. itself and over its individual members?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was quite clear: Milosevic was the overall ruler of Serbia, and absolutely nobody could even have dreamt of doing anything otherwise, contrary to him. Everything had to be done as he instructed, according to his instructions and under his control. So in actual fact, this applied not only to the government but also to the parliament, until the multi-party elections took place where he didn't have complete control but nonetheless he had most of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can clarify that for us who weren't there at the time, Mr. Markovic. Can you give us an example of the way in which that control demonstrated itself and the ways in which you came to the conclusion that Mr. Milosevic was the overall ruler and had absolute control in -- in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be easier to find evidence and proof that that was not so, rather than that was so, because the whole life of Serbia and its communication with others was conceived in such a way and constructed in such a way that it was in fact wholly -- all Serbia's institutions had to behave wholly according to the dictates of Milosevic. He didn't have a legal foundation for that, but that was what it was like in actual fact, in reality. And if he didn't agree with anything, then he would organise popular demonstrations, he would get together hundreds of people, and then would have somebody replaced. So that didn't happen once; it happened umpteen times, and that is quite obvious. He would gather together 100.000 people, and you can see the tapes of that, with the cameras and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you have any personal experience of that absolute control being demonstrated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I kept in communication with the government of Serbia, just as I did with the governments of the other republics. That was my duty and task. And everything that Milosevic said was put into practice by his Prime Ministers and his ministers. I never encountered a single instance of anybody saying anything different, or even dared to think differently. So those communications were very intense. And I always knew exactly what his representatives would advocate at the meetings. It couldn't differ in one iota from what Milosevic said. And even if they were given counter-arguments, they would be like parrots, repeating one and the same things. And they weren't always that intelligent either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you'd care to follow that and we could have some concrete examples, it might be helpful, but it's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I can first of all approach it in the negative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever experience anybody advancing an argument or a position counter to that of the accused and succeeding with his position, succeeding in, as it were, arguing against the accused?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean somebody from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: A person like that wouldn't have kept his post for 24 hours had he done so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what would assist the Court would be if you can think now or at any stage in your evidence of concrete examples of people in high office or comparatively high office being as controlled by the accused as you have described. We'll come back to it a little later before I sit down, but if you think of any example now or if you think of any as we're looking at any other bits of the evidence, perhaps you'll alert us to us and we can hear from you about it. Before we part from this very general issue, the issue of the accused's approach --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: All the Prime Ministers of Serbia behaved that way. For example, when communicating with me, at all times Radmilovic and other Prime Ministers - I can give you their names - Bozovic, another instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about those who were expressing views counter to your economic reforms and democratisation programme? Were they, in your judgement, people expressing views of free will, or were they acting or instructions, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were both, of course. It was enough for a general negative position to prevail, and then of course everybody would have the right to add to it and embroider based on their own thinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other topic about the accused's general performance: As people sustained injuries and losses and bereavements, did he ever, to you, show or was he ever seen to show understanding or sympathy of the losses that people were suffering as a result of these wars?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In what way do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sometimes rulers -- leaders go and see the injured in hospitals or go and show their sympathy to individuals. Did he ever do that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to the other more particular point a little later. Paragraph 27 of the latest statement emerging from proofing and not from the earlier statement. The Brioni declaration July in 1991, was it an initiation of whom, yours?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The Brioni declaration emerged from the various discussions held at the Brioni Islands with the representatives of the republics and provinces taking part. However, in preparing that meeting, I myself inaugurated at our government meeting that our government should prepare a proposal on the so-called three-month moratorium. I, first of all, wanted this to be six months, thought about six months, because we had very profound problems, so in my opinion, we should have had six months to be able to deal with the situation and bring it up to the level of being able, on a legal basis, logically, without any bloodshed, to implement all the decisions that were made. If we were supposed to scatter and go our separate ways, that that should be done without any bloodshed. But we thought that nobody would accept this, so we suggested a three-month moratorium. And that moratorium found its place in the Brioni declaration, and as the federal government, we took it upon ourselves to prepare all the elements that would enable, within that three-month moratorium period, to create a situation which would enable the functioning of our society, at least at a minimum level, minimum conditions. And then after that, that decisions could be taken which would not mean leading to war or further conflict. And I must say, that we waited over a month for a Presidency meeting to be convened and to have a debate pursuant to our proposal. And when the proposal was actually made, then the same tendencies became evident; one side considered that the proposal was insufficient and that it should be -- that the functions of the Federation should be strengthened of this joint state, joint country. That was the group led by Milosevic. And the other stream that thought things should be left more loosely, and that stream was led by Kucan. But anyway, that three-month moratorium, which was designed to assist matters and to help us allow society to function at a minimum level, to prevent further erosion and a complete disintegration of everything, which would mean anarchy and the struggle of everybody against everybody else, this general uprising, unfortunately it wasn't able to form its function. The war followed, first with Croatia and then with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You set out as well how you gave advice to Vance after the declaration in which you expected by way of bloodshed and how many troops would be required to stop that. And I needn't take you through that in any more detail. The Chamber will know that the Brioni declaration has already been exhibited, Exhibit 330, tab 35. I don't ask to look at it for the time being. In paragraph 29, originally from the proofing session, I think in that second half of 1991 and as a matter of detail you actually suggested 13 new laws. So you were still actively pursuing the job of government. But only three of them, and you think the least important or significant three, were adopted, the rest being blocked by the accused and his representatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of that three-month moratorium, for us to be able to implement the basic proposals of the Federal Executive Council or, rather, their ideas as to how the state could function, these laws were proposed and only three sporadic ones were adopted, the rest weren't, of the 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal with another incident: In October 1991 at, I think, apart -- for private family reasons you went to Zagreb, you were called by Tudjman to a meeting, he asked you to talk to Mesic, and the result was that the three of you, prime minister and two presidents, found yourselves in the presidential palace when the palace was bombed.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just want to ask you a question. The bomb, as was subsequently discovered, was sent from a very high-flying aircraft. And did it come to a position very close to where the three of you had been having lunch?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I had talks which lasted roughly four and a half hours in the so-called Banski Dvori, the palace in Zagreb. And there was a cabinet there, a set of offices of Franjo Tudjman. And in a more -- in another section of the building, Mesic had his office there too. I was in communication with both of them, and Tudjman organised a joint lunch. After that luncheon, Mesic, Tudjman, and myself went to his office - Tudjman's office, I mean - and we started discussing how we could use the elements of the Brioni delegation and the moratorium in general to solve the situation in the most peaceful way. When we started talking -- we'd just got through a few sentences, I think. We were having a conversation and speaking about Mesic going back to Belgrade. He hadn't been to Belgrade for a long time and that the ministers from Croatia should also go back to Belgrade. At one point, Tudjman even phoned Kucan to have a -- talk to him about that. And when they started their conversation, there was an explosion. Several missiles exploded that were shot, and two or three planes were flying at a height of 14 to 15 kilometres and one of them fell quite near the dining room in which we were having lunch a few minutes before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been gathered together, the three of you, long enough for information to be sent back outside Croatia to another state and for an aircraft to be activated to send this plane to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And it is interesting to note that Tudjman had his office, his cabinet, he had had it there for months. Mesic had had his offices there for months, and they hadn't been shelled, bombed. The bombing took place when I was there, and I was there for about four and a half hours, which yes, was sufficient time to send information from Zagreb to Belgrade and to send planes out. They were the fastest type of aircraft. The assumption is that they were the MiG-29 type aircraft that can fly at very high altitudes. General Tus, who used to be the commander of the air force, said that there were only three pilots capable of flying at such high altitudes and targeting targets with such precision. And had we remained in the dining room, I wouldn't be sitting here with you today most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 33. Towards the end of 1991, just so we can have a picture of your life and position, were you being threatened from both Serbia and Croatia? From the Serbian perspective, you were being said to be an Ustasha; from the Croatian perspective, you were being seen to be pro-Serb in orientation. Just yes if I've got that right.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was demonised by both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A word about Kosovo, paragraph 34, from proofing. Your relationship with persons in Kosovo was -- was good during your time as Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I advocated autonomy for Kosovo such as it had had during Tito's time. For this reason, I was attacked by both Jovic and Milosevic. I was on good terms with the president of the executive board of Kosovo, Jusuf Zegnullahi, who was threatened with liquidation and had to flee abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how he was threatened or who threatened him?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, threats are not made by someone threatening in public. This is done by creating a network of threats around a person which prevents him from functioning normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that we have the picture of Kosovo at this early stage, was it safe for you to travel to Kosovo at that stage or not? That's 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I did go to Kosovo in 1989 and in 1990 on several occasions, but in 1991 I didn't go any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was too risky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the level of police presence in Kosovo at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There were large numbers of policemen, primarily from Serbia but also from other parts of Yugoslavia, because there was a Presidency conclusion, with which I disagreed, that a police unit should be sent from the federal reserve police force, so to say, to keep law and order there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraphs 37 and following deal with military activity until the end of 1991 but, very briefly, can you just confirm, please, that as to events in Slovenia the first you knew of these was when you were telephoned on the 26th of June at 4.00 in the morning by Kucan. You asked him why he called you and not the Presidency since the JNA was not under your jurisdiction. He said he was unable to reach the Presidency; you called Kadijevic, who was at the Main Staff, and he confirmed that the army in Slovenia had been brought out of their barracks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at a government meeting with Kadijevic present, you explaining that you would have objected to military intervention, although you couldn't have prevented it, he replying that that was the reason why you hadn't been reformed, he then saying that you would never return to the government cabinet again. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I intervened and asked why use had been made of my name, although no one had talked to me and I had not given approval to anyone to do this. Kadijevic answered, "Well, because we knew you wouldn't agree, we didn't even ask."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it was your understanding of the constitution that the army was not allowed to make decisions without decisions of the Presidency, a political decision being taken and for which a majority was required.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. The Presidency never made this decision, nor was the Presidency ever asked about this. I had a long talk about this with Jovic, who claimed that it was the army's duty to do that, but the use of the army was exclusively within the competence of the Presidency, and it was insisted on the fact that the Presidency should proclaim a state of emergency that would allow the army to intervene, but the Presidency was split. Milosevic's group was in favour; the others were against. It was four against four. So the army could not be used. In this case, it was done without the approval of the Presidency. Of course, they tried to use this against the Federal Executive Council, as if it could have given such approval at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard a little about the use of the air force over Ljubljana some days after this. Paragraph 39 and paragraph 25 of the original. Did you invite Kadijevic to your cabinet on learning of this and say that if he was going to bomb Ljubljana he was going to bomb you, since you were going to go there to stop what you described as a ridiculous war? Were you advised by your own Ministry of Interior or, rather, Croatia's Ministry of Interior not to go because of the risk of your being liquidated, and were you advised further by Stjepan Mesic not to go, but despite all that, did you go to Ljubljana --

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- having talks with some of his "young Turks," as he described them, and without whom he seemed decision inclined to talk?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't he who called them that; I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. My mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned that the army was preparing to send all its air force against Ljubljana, which would certainly have destroyed Ljubljana. The people in Ljubljana discovered that the entire leadership was in shelters, so I set out for Ljubljana and I told Kadijevic, "If you bomb Ljubljana, you'll be bombing me." A team spent the night with me and this reads like a thriller. We travelled from Belgrade to Zagreb and then from Zagreb to Ljubljana by car. In Ljubljana, we were met with machine-guns pointed at us at the ready, but we did manage to stop the further escalation of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia - paragraph 41, 26 in the original - the withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia by the Presidency was something over which you had no right to vote, and I think you say that was under the influence of the accused?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did Mesic and Tupurkovski take?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mesic and Tupurkovski were against this. And after this session we met in my office to analyse the consequences of such a decision, especially as it was clear that the army was to withdraw from Slovenia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, which meant that there was going to be an enormous concentration of army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we already knew that part of the future war on this territory was to take place there. Mesic, to be sure, was afraid that part of the army would remain in Croatia, but this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraphs 42 and 43, paragraph 27 in the original. A word or so about the accused's relationship with Jovic, having in mind the time. What was the relationship between the two of them like?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They worked as a team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An example; the demonstrations of the opposition on the 9th of March of 1991, was Milosevic at risk of losing power then? And if so, what did Jovic do?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a lot of evidence as to the way in which the two of them worked as a team. What you are referring to now are events that happened in March of 1991, when the citizens of Belgrade went out into the streets and demonstrated against Milosevic. The army went out into the streets then with tanks. I was in Zagreb at the time, not in Belgrade, because this happened during the weekend, and I knew nothing about it. Later, at the session we had in Belgrade, Jovic said that he had received approval by telephone from the other members of the Presidency. As for me, I then held my well-known speech in the Presidency, saying that the tanks should be withdrawn to the barracks. This was published in the press, and for this reason I came under attack in the Presidency of Yugoslavia. Jovic then resigned because attempts were underway to declare a state of emergency. And when this did not succeed after several attempts, Jovic resigned. And then Milosevic gave a dramatic speech on television in which he said, among other things, that he did not recognise the federal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. units for this reason and because a situation had now arisen in which there was no Presidency, because the president had resigned. The other members of the Presidency who were under Milosevic's control were also resigned. And to avoid a hiatus of power and to prevent the possibility of the army being used against everybody else, Tupurkovski, who was the Vice-President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and I agreed in my cabinet to call the remainder of the Presidency, Drnovsek, Bogicevic, Mesic, and of course Tupurkovski. I also attended and we declared that there was not a hiatus, that there was an institution that was still functioning. After this Jovic and the other members of the Presidency who had resigned came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving now to a different topic, paramilitaries, very briefly. Paragraph 46, which emerges from proofing, not from the earlier statement. Were you when you were here a few weeks ago asked to review a statement of the accused reported in a newspaper to be found at tab 11 of Exhibit 570, headed "I ordered mobilisation"?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be good enough to go to the English version, and rather than read all of it, the third page in the second complete paragraph we find a passage that reads: "I deem that despite the new circumstances in Yugoslavia there is no need to introduce emergency measures in the Republic of Serbia. All institutions of the system and the entire life in the republic ought to follow the normal course. The citizens can rest assured that the Republic of Serbia is in a position to provide the protection of interests of the republic of all its citizens and the Serbian people." Now, having -- that's one passage. On the previous page perhaps was the passage I should have taken you to first. Towards the bottom of the page, the last complete paragraph: "In the present circumstances of attempting to incite disorder in Sandzak and in Kosovo and Metohija, I ordered mobilisation of the reserve task force of the Serbian Ministry of Defence security forces and the urgent forming of the supplementary forces of the Republic of Serbia police." Having read that article, which I've just read a couple of passages, what comments do you make about the accused's actions at that time and his ability to control armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember well that at the time I wrote an open letter to Slobodan Milosevic in which I demanded that he withdraw this decision and in which I listed all the dangers ensuing from such a decision. I haven't got the text with me, but as far as I remember I concluded that unfortunately we are living in a time where it is far easier and safer to advocate war than to advocate peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which year again, Mr. Nice, please, the 16th of March I see is the date. Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's 1991 for the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The letter, I think, comes later and is in September, September the 30th. I'm grateful to Ms. Tromp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in any position - paragraph 47 - to do anything about paramilitaries insofar as you were aware of them, or was that outside your competence?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was completely outside the competence of the Federal Executive Council because everything that had to do with the army and the paramilitary units was directly within the competence of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I should have asked you, what was the accused's and Kadijevic's personal relationship like? Did they get on well together or not? Paragraph 48, and I think also in earlier paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not always the same. Before I took up my post in Belgrade, Milosevic and Kadijevic communicated well. They went on vacation together in a place near Dubrovnik, and I have to admit I learnt a lot later, that Kadijevic had suggested to the then-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Mr. Dizdarevic, that Milosevic should be given the mandate of forming the new government. At the time I formed the government and in the first period, communication with Kadijevic was relatively good, and Kadijevic tried to prove that he was adhering to the reform programme, especially the part that related to stabilisation. But as things went on and as the programme never ended in stabilisation but in political changes, changes in government, changes in private property and so on, our ways diverged, and then there were problems in the relations between the republics in Yugoslavia and relations between Kadijevic and me cooled more and more, until they finally declined completely. And as relations between Kadijevic and me cooled, so they got better and better between Kadijevic and Milosevic, and in the end they got on together very well. But they cooperated throughout this time. In some periods, however, communication between Kadijevic and me overcame or was better at times than the communication between Kadijevic and Milosevic. And this can be seen from our communication. We would agree about something with Kadijevic, and later on he would change his mind. Kadijevic and I would sometimes talk for hours and exchange views, analyse the situation, make comparisons. And when I managed to convince him that drastic measures should not be taken and that things should not be done that would only deepen the crisis and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to conclude this passage, paragraph 49. In the same way as you'd received an offer from the accused to become president of a re-formed structure in the fall of 1990, in the beginning of 1991, did Kadijevic raise with you a possibility which would have put you at the head of government? And head of state, actually?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In contrast to Milosevic's earlier proposal, which I didn't take at all seriously, because there was no basis for such a plan to be implemented, after the first sessions that were held about declaring a state of emergency in Yugoslavia and giving the army certain powers to act, when this fell through, there was a period I think in early January 1991 when Kadijevic came to see me with a proposal that had been developed, as he said, in the General Staff. They suggested carrying out a campaign because at the time there were units of the JNA all over Yugoslavia, so they developed a project according to which the leadership of Croatia, headed by Tudjman, and the leadership of Slovenia, headed by Kucan, should all be arrested. And if they resisted, one knew what would happen to them. As Kadijevic was unable to obtain approval in the Presidency, he tried another route; he asked me whether I would agree for them to do this. And as they would be doing it without the approval of the Presidency and bypassing the Presidency and they would in fact be replacing the Presidency, if I supported this plan, because I was the prime minister and the senior executive official at the level of the Federation, I would be made president. He pulled out a bundle of papers to show me this plan, and I asked him not to show it to me. I said, "You seem to think you're going to solve the Yugoslav crisis in this way." He said, "Yes." I said, "You have named Kucan, you have named Tudjman, what about Milosevic?" And he said to me -- he jumped up and said, "Milosevic is the only one fighting for Yugoslavia and who would back this up if it wasn't for him?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, just a gentle reminder on time, if you can bring this passage to a conclusion with how it ended, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, I declined this. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you -- in March, Kadijevic travelled to the Soviet Union- paragraph 50 - without informing you. Matters between you got worse in June. You asked for his resignation at one session of the government, but he could only be dismissed by the Assembly, which didn't meet, and he had further support from the Presidency. And he sent his deputy, Admiral Brovet, or one of his assistants. And we can see reference to your seeking the resignation of both Kadijevic and Brovet in tab 12. I'm not going to go through it in detail -- at tab 12, which is a Vreme article of the September the 23rd of 1991. And you've reviewed that and can answer questions about it if anyone wants to ask you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring to a letter of protest to Milosevic about partial mobilisation, is that to be found in our tab 13? And it's in fact the letter of the 30th of September of 1991. It's here again simply reported in a newspaper. You were under the impression we had a copy of the letter itself, and it may be we have, and if so we've mislaid it, but at the moment we're dependent upon this newspaper report of your letter of protest to the accused. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote an open letter to Mr. Milosevic, asking him not to do what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, mobilisation at that stage was, so far as you were concerned, unlawful.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I come to the last couple of questions, which are going to be about intercepts, can we go back to the question that His Honour Judge May asked you earlier, examples of the accused exercising complete control over other individuals. Have you been able - I know it's difficult when you're answering questions to think of something else - but have you been stimulated to think of any other examples or any particular examples of how he exercised such complete control?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, formally it was the Assembly who elected Prime Ministers, but it was he who designated them, and they did exactly what he asked. There was no difference, not even in nuances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, did you review a number of recordings of telephone intercepts when you were last here in The Hague a few weeks ago and did you sign a document to the effect that you'd listened to those intercepted telephone conversations, identifying voices of participants as revealed on the table that accompanies the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps he can have this before him, just to look at it.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I did listen to them, and apart from one voice, I recognised all the voices, and I have signed all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're referred to, I think, on only one of the intercepts yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber will be good enough to give an exhibit number to the certificate producing the transcripts and to the transcripts themselves. The witness is himself referred to only in tab 3 of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in tab 3, on the first page, at the foot of the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you're producing a number of tapes here, are you, intercepts, as well as the certificate?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am in the Court's hands. I'm afraid I've actually forgotten the precise routine we've been pursuing. I know that whatever happens, the intercepts are produced for identification only at this stage, because they all have to be produced in order to show their provenance later. The important evidence, of course, is the evidence of the identification of voices, so far as this witness is concerned. That could conveniently be done by production of this entire exhibit, which has the transcripts of the intercepts attached to it or, alternatively, just by the certificate and the accompanying table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The certificate obviously can be produced. But these, I suspect, are tapes which have already been produced, haven't they, and marked for identification? Or are they new tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think these are new ones. These are new ones, because they haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are new ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think so. But they haven't yet been -- His Honour Judge Kwon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They have an exhibit number here. 35.28. Some are and some are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, could you during the adjournment sort that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because I think there will be difficulty in due course with these tapes if we don't get them in one place and organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a consolidation exercise under way at the moment for putting all the tapes together and having them tabulated in a uniform way, so that the important point is the certificate and the table from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I suggest that the simplest way to deal with this would be to have -- to give the certificate an exhibit number, the attached transcripts will be marked for identification, and when we come back, perhaps you can tell us which of these have been produced and which haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we have it on the record. We'll have a number now for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The certificate, Your Honour, is 571.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just looking at tab 3, which is a conversation on the 4th of September of 1991 between Karadzic and the accused, and at the foot of the page when the accused's spoken of speaking to Alija, who he alleges was behaving badly and would not come over to talk, Karadzic says here his ideas. "He is expecting the Berlin Congress. I told him openly that the Berlin Congress is not possible any more." And he goes on a bit. And then in the middle of this block of text: "Fine. I will probably be more clever after The Hague. But his opinion is that Europe will force Croatia and Slovenia to stay in Yugoslavia. He thinks he has some information that such pressure is already being made and that they will first put pressure on them to stay in the Federation. If not, they will try to leave. Keep Yugoslavia the way it is. In some -- some boundaries, but in loose connections. That is the line of thinking of Ante Markovic. He is hoping for that. However, we -- in that case, we don't accept -- we want to have strong ties with the federal state." Mr. Markovic, was this a true and accurate reflection of your opinions at that time or not; some boundaries but in a loose connection?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: If we're talking about boundaries within the country, then yes. But frontiers or borders towards the outside, no. What I understand this to be is boundaries within Yugoslavia. So yes, loose connections. I thought it was better for us to have any kind of connection rather than none at all, and so that is my thinking fairly accurately interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich informs me, and I'm sorry not to have understood this earlier, when the documents were so well prepared for me by Ms. Dicklich, that the intercepts already tendered are not in the bundle but are in the spreadsheet and so therefore the ones in the bundle are the new ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, we'd better have them marked for identification with a separate exhibit number. Two of them have been, I notice, exhibited before. But I think let's at this stage simply give the next -- to give them all a separate exhibit number marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 572, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Markovic, just to return to something that we've touched on already and that is dealt with but in a summary way at paragraph 61 of your latest signed statement. The pressure of the accused's -- of the things the accused said being consistent with or inconsistent with what he was doing or subsequently to do. Can you just help us a little bit more with that. You said something about it, but to what extent -- what was it, a trait, that his actions belie his words?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on who he was talking to. As you can see, when he's talking to Karadzic, he's saying exactly what he's thinking, because he's trying to arrange things with him. Whereas, what he discussed with me, there was a certain amount of reservation in this regard, always had to think what was behind it all, what he was actually thinking. So it was always a fact of him thinking one thing and saying another. So you would have to give the whole thing a lot of thought if you were to know what his true intentions really were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm reminded that you haven't in a sense answered the whole question. Thinking and saying is another thing. What was he doing? How did that fit with what he had said?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. He would say one thing and do another. And his acts were different. He would say that he was fighting for Yugoslavia; whereas, in actual fact he was fighting for something different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you say he was fighting for?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He never actually told me, but it was quite obvious that he was fighting for a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now before cross-examination. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I begin with my cross-examination, I just wish to say that a moment ago I was given a new plan, a new schedule for the witnesses, or list of witnesses, as of the beginning of next week, and it is radically different from what we were given a few days ago. I really would like to protest because by constantly changing the order of witnesses leads to confusion, and quite simply makes it impossible for me to work normally. I don't see that with all the machinery the other side has at its disposal that they can't stick to a schedule. You can compare the two and you'll see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a change of order between 1345 and 1780, I see that, and there's one additional witness, it seems, 1448 to -- yes. Mr. Milosevic, we bear that in mind. One advantage of our abbreviated sittings, though, is that you will have more time for preparation and won't be under the pressure which you were when we were sitting for such long hours. And we invite the Prosecution, of course, to keep these changes to an absolute minimum that's necessary. Mr. Nice, I'm sure you have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have it in mind at all times. It's, of course, difficult for witnesses to schedule themselves into the three-day week. We're all doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Markovic, I shall do my best to use my time as rationally as possible; however, let me begin with some questions which you dealt with at the end of your testimony and for which we even have documents here which shows that the situation has been portrayed quite incorrectly. Is it at issue, Mr. Markovic, that you were the man who made the decision to involve the army, engage the army, at the beginning of the Yugoslav conflicts and clashes or, rather, the man who caused the war in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. And in the decision of the Federal Executive Council, which relates to infringement of the boundaries by Slovenia and taken over the borders, it says that the Federal Secretary for the Interior is duty-bound to coordinate with Slovenia and, if the needs arises, that he can utilise that part which was on the so-called green line; that is to say, the people in the army protecting the borders. So never anywhere in any of the documents does it refer to the deployment of the army. And I spoke about this at a number of meetings, including the fact that as was common knowledge, at a meeting of the Federal Executive Council or Yugoslav government - I've already said that and there are documents to back this up - I dealt with this issue and discussed it with Veljko Kadijevic and there was absolutely no permission given for him to deploy the army. And I couldn't have given him permission to do so anyway, because permission for the deployment of the army is something that the Presidency alone could give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the point, that the Presidency did not give permission for the deployment of the army and because the president of the then-Presidency, Mr. Borisav Jovic, knew absolutely nothing about the deployment of the army, and you knew that full well.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I had no idea either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, whether you had an idea or not is another matter. I'm going to ask you a few questions, and I have grounds for asking them. In the stenograms from the session of the 21st of August 1991, the session commenced at 11.00 of the Presidency of the SFRY. And you attended that Presidency meeting, as did I myself, and the president of Slovenia, Milan Kucan too, and of course all the other members. I don't have time to enumerate all their names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is the stenogram that I'm referring to, Mr. May. Part of it exists in the big binder that I was provided with, but there's no tab number. All I have here is a portion of those. R0006543 is the number. And I'm going to quote from that. Could this document be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have the document? Have you got a copy of it or you only have one copy there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my own copy; however, it is a document from Mr. Nice -- or rather, it is a transcript of the Presidency session, and I was disclosed it by the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose they could put their hands on it immediately. No doubt searches can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You'll have to get on for the moment without it, Mr. Milosevic, because there's only one copy, which you have. What is it that you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm going to quote certain portions from that shorthand transcript. Just let me see it in the binder. I've been given a binder here with respect to the witness which contains part of that shorthand transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and extract it from the binder to give the witness a copy. I have another copy for myself. I don't know whether this is the entire document, but I'll begin from here and the witness can follow. The pages have been marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is on page 239 of the stenographic notes. It is a Presidency session of the 21st of August, 1991. And in the middle of that page, it says: "Ante Markovic --" this is how you begin: "I nevertheless think that we have to say something with respect to the functioning of the borders, regardless of the fact that it is not a purely economic matter but it is also an economic category." And Gligorov goes on to ask something and your answer is "absolutely so." And then we come to Slobodan Milosevic speaking, yes. And on page 4, it says, it quotes the lack of respect for this decision of the Federal Executive Council with respect to the payment of customs revenues. And I end the quotation there. And I say to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may have got -- we may have got the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can help. 427, tab 6 -- the English page. But if it starts on page 239 of -- of the B/C/S, it should be about three pages in from the back of the English, which will be roughly at the foot, page 7 or thereabouts, I should suspect, but perhaps if we hear the text read out we'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was quoting your document, the one on the table, and I say, and I'm quoting from the stenographic notes now: "On the basis of this approach, you began the war in Slovenia. About customs, dues, and borders, customs mostly." So that was common knowledge at that time, wasn't it, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I never said that. Quite the contrary. I do remember this meeting, and you said two or three times that I had started the war against Slovenia, and Kucan said something along those lines as well. But at that same meeting I pulled out a document and read from it. It was a government decision. Nowhere does it say there that the army can be used. That does not exist anywhere. And there is no evidence at all that the Prime Minister of the federal government gave any instructions along those lines because he couldn't have given it. But documents do exist, however, which testify to the fact that there was a sharp clash between the minister of the army, or national defence, whichever you like to call it, and the Prime Minister about that question, and the Prime Minister went to Slovenia to stop that completely useless war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That it was completely useless is quite clear. Now, that it was highly detrimental, that is very clear too. But let me remind you what the then-president of Slovenia, Milan Kucan says. And you can turn the page, it is page 243 of these stenographic notes, and it begins with Kucan. It says, Milan Kucan speaking, "I don't want to be held responsible before the Prime Minister and answer to him who quite obviously wants, now that he has lost the war, to win all that." And then he goes on to discuss other matters. I'll skip over those to save time, but that is not only what I claim in the quotation that I read out, which is a quotation by me, but that is what Milan Kucan, president of Slovenia also says. On the next page, on page 244, when he refers to your explanations and your request to have two members from the Slovenian government returned to the government, in that middle paragraph on page 244, he says the following -- I'm beginning with the beginning of the sentence, not the beginning of the paragraph, to save time: "I don't have to convince you that you're not going to find a single man in Slovenia, including these two here, who would go back to the Federal Executive Council, the SIV, or rather, the government, Yugoslav government, and to work in the government. It is a Federal Executive Council which we all know about in Slovenia and we know that it began the war in Slovenia." And that is what Kucan says. Is that being contested, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean is it being contested what Kucan said or what the facts are or were? What Kucan said is one thing, and the facts are something else again. Nowhere do you speak when I reacted and said, "I've had enough of those accusations. I'm going to read out what the government decision says with respect to customs dues, and it will emerge that nobody had the right to deploy the army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll help you.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can, but I can't find that here. Now, as to what Kucan said, those were political games that suited him at the time. It suited him to say that at that time. But nowhere did he say that he called me up in the morning and asked me to help him stop the army to march forward, although I couldn't do anything because it didn't come under my power and authority. And did the army ever act pursuant to anybody else's orders except those of the Presidency of Yugoslavia? Nobody's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this case here, it acted according to yours. On page 246, it begins and says, "Ante Markovic." So that is where you refute what Kucan is saying. Now, how you refute him can be seen from the actual quotation. You are quoting your decision, and this is what you say.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 247. You haven't got page 247? I gave you everything that I received in the binder, but it's the same stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page has the ERN number, Mr. May, 00526240. So I'm now quoting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can find it. I don't seem able to find the passage. Just read it out for the moment while we look for it. Just read it out slowly to the witness so he can follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 247.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Court something in the meantime, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, am I the accused here or am I a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, don't -- don't be offended, Mr. Markovic, if you're asked questions by the accused. There's no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no question of you being offended or anything like that. He is entitled to ask questions. And if he asks things which are improper or unfair or prejudicial, he'll be stopped. But he's entitled to put his case to the witnesses, and that is what he's doing. If you don't agree with him, just simply say no. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm quoting you, Mr. Markovic, because you are responding to Kucan and explaining the decision. You say, "The decision brought in by the Federal Executive Council in which members of the Federal Executive Council from Slovenia took part. And they have now written out their resignations, so the decision that was made after Slovenia took over by a single act the borders and by a single act it took over the customs as well and a single act control of flights. All this was done by their own one-sided acts, without acquiescence from anybody. The Federal Executive Council has made the decision on the immediate implementation of federal rules and regulations with respect to borders and taking over borders in the Republic of Slovenia." I'm going to read it out because there are just two paragraphs. And to be fair towards you, I'm reading your decision, the decision of the Federal Executive Council as quoted by you from these stenographic notes, quotation marks placed here and you read the decision, which reads as follows: "In order to ensure that federal regulations are being adhered to with respect to our outside borders and the movement of the populace, the Federal Secretariat --" I keep losing the interpretation, so I don't know if I'm speaking too quickly for the interpreters. But anyway, "The Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs will directly ensure the control of border crossings." And then you go on to comment and say, "So the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs has been given that assignment. And then you go on to quote, secondly: "In order to provide for the implementation of federal rules and regulations --" Yes, I do understand that the interpreters don't have the documents. I'm being cautioned to speak more slowly. I shall do my best to do so to help the interpreters interpret. But you're quoting the decision: "In order to implement federal rules with respect to border crossings, the Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs will realise direct cooperation with the Federal Secretariat of National Defence in order to engage border units of the JNA, in order to provide security for the state borders at border crossings and in built-up areas in the border belt." So you are saying there that the decision that you made does not involve the deployment of the army and that you didn't do; whereas, here it says that they will cooperate with the army and engage frontier units of the JNA to provide security for the border and border belt. That is what you yourself state. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said myself a moment ago. The border units, frontier units, are there to secure the frontiers, the borders, and nothing more than that. So tell me, please, where you can find a single document which states that the army in Slovenia should leave the barracks with tanks and to move around with the different units and to take control of certain regions of Slovenia. You will not find that stated anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't enter into the details of the federal government decision; that is to say, whether they would deploy tanks and leave the barracks with tanks or arms or without arms. All you say is that the units should be deployed and the units are deployed according to their establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are not paying attention, I suggest, to the words. The words said "To engage border units in order to provide security for the state borders or border crossings." Now, if you're going to quote documents, you must quote them accurately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did quote it accurately, Mr. May, word for word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you're putting -- are you putting -- so that the witness can understand it, are you suggesting that this was an order for the JNA to go beyond the borders, to attack other parts of Slovenia? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I'm suggesting. I'm saying that this is an order to have the army activated in Slovenia, that the army that was stationed in Slovenia, anyway, should be activated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us -- wait a moment. We -- now we understand the suggestion. We'll put it to the witness. Mr. Markovic, what the accused is suggesting is that this was an order to activate the army in Slovenia. Is that the case or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It cannot be correct. The Federal Executive Council has no jurisdiction over the armed forces. The Federal Executive Council did have jurisdiction over certain police units, and those that had to do with border patrols and border crossings and customs duties. The Federal Executive Council concluded that in order to protect the borders of Yugoslavia, the police should be activated and - which is quite logical - that it should cooperate. This is not an order to the armed forces. It cannot be an order to the armed forces. It's order to the police, that they should cooperate with the border units inside the green belt, nothing further than that, nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you have just quoted the decision which reads, literally, that "They will cooperate with the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, that is, the armed forces, in order to activate the border units of the JNA" and so on and so forth. So activating JNA units. Look at page 249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the document and I think it's futile to go on arguing about it. We can read it and we will draw our own conclusions from that. You've heard what the witness has said about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The registry have confirmed that the exhibit is 427, tab 6, but there's no other copy in court at the moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, would you then, please, comment what Milan Kucan, the President of Slovenia said on that occasion in connection with your quoting this decision. He says: "Milan Kucan:" -- I'll read everything he said, because it's very brief. "Secondly, as for the conclusion you have read --" that's the one I quoted -- "there was a debate while Zivko Pregl," who was a member from Slovenia, "protested against using this conclusion for the purposes for which it was used. If you didn't know to what this conclusion would lead, that's your problem. Objectively this is what it led to. Look, we have at our disposal and the comrades from the Secretariat for National Defence can show you how this was implemented in particular commands and orders." They were referring to your conclusions, so how can you say it's none of your business? And then Ante Markovic says, "I'm sorry, but that has nothing to do with it." Milan Kucan: How do you mean it has nothing to do with it? You are the president of the Federal Executive Council who signed this and this was the occasion for the resignation of --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name of the official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This conclusion led to the intervention of the armed forces in Slovenia, and Milan Kucan and Zivko Pregl, the member from Slovenia of the federal government, who resigned for this reason, also said this. And you, Mr. Markovic, are saying that you had nothing to do with your order -- your conclusion being implemented and nobody else knew about this in the Presidency. Is this in dispute, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely is it in dispute. Not only is it in dispute, it is incorrect. Zivko Pregl handed me his written resignation in which he said that he was asked in Slovenia to resign. Unfortunately, I don't have all these documents. I am doing everything based on my recollection. And this has nothing to do with what we are talking about. Whether Zivko Pregl resigned because he disagreed or because he was forced in Slovenia to do this, that's the question. In his resignation to me, in his letter of resignation, all it says is that he was asked in Slovenia to resign, and that actually is not anything that proves something in this respect. And if Mr. Milosevic has no better arguments than these, don't let him use them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, what you said is about something I quoted that Milan Kucan said, that you created the war in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has already dealt with that, so let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you were at the head of the federal government at the time Slovenia declared independence and at the time Croatia declared independence and when this war that you caused in Slovenia began and when conflicts broke out in Slovenia -- in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are not to put matters which are in dispute. He's dealt with the war in Slovenia. He's denied completely that he had anything to do with it. So for you to put it tendentiously as though he were responsible is wrong. Now, what you can do is put questions, not argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I quite tendentiously and correctly quoted Mr. Markovic, who was quoting his own decision activating the JNA. Yes, tendentiously, with a tendention towards establishing the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not concerned directly with Slovenia in this case. We've now spent about half an hour on it. So let's move on to something which is more relevant and involves your case. The witness gave quite a lot of evidence involving you, and you may want to ask him about that, if you challenge it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I will put all the questions I consider relevant, Mr. May. The witness is testifying to events up to December 1991, and that's the period I'm asking him about, not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were at the head of the federal government when the break-up of Yugoslavia began, up to the end of 1991; is this correct, Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 16 of your statement, you say that I had de facto control over the government of Serbia. There's no need to go into that now, but is it in dispute that you had both de jure and de facto control over the federal government, both at the time of these large-scale exoduses of the Serbs and the events that led to the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I had control over the government up to the end of 1960. After that, the competencies of the government were reduced and little by little its scope of activity was reduced. And ultimately, the members of the government who started working together as a single team on a programme of reform and democratisation and change in our society, that was a single team at the time, as the nationalisms grew, whether they were separatist or nationalist with a tendency to expansion, they all started working more and more under instructions from their own republics and less and less as members of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it in dispute that you had both de jure and de facto control over the time I am charged with the shelling of Dubrovnik, the events in Vukovar? Throughout this time, you were the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: But the Prime Minister had no competency and no power over the armed forces, none whatsoever. So nothing that concerned the activities of the armed forces was something I could affect. But what you had with Kadijevic, that did affect the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were the Prime Minister and had the de facto and de jure control over the federal government, why when you say that meetings with Kadijevic and members of the Presidency took place in your office and, as you say, you even heard some intercepts, doesn't that mean that you had all the strings of power in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This was not at the time when Slovenia and Croatia seceded. That was before. But under the constitution, the Yugoslav government had very modest competencies. The things that happened, including your breaking into the monetary system of Yugoslavia and the other things that you did, such as blocking goods from Slovenia and so on, by these actions you brought into question even these modest competencies of the federal government. You mounted an attack on these competencies. But I did whatever I could, however futile. I went to the Assembly of Slovenia to get agreement from them and not to take any radical measures. I also gave a speech in the Croatian parliament. I won't say how I was greeted there. I asked you to let me speak in the parliament of Serbia but was never given permission to do this. Look at the speech I held in the Croatian parliament, where among other things I said, "This is the first and last time I am speaking as a Croat. I am not the same kind of Croat that you are because you hate Serbs and others because you are Croats. That's not the case with me." I told Tudjman a long time ago, and I repeated that before the parliament, "Don't talk to the Serbs in Croatia through Belgrade, through Milosevic, because that will end in war. Talk to them directly. Sit down with them and talk." I also said to him, and repeated this before the Croatian parliament - and there are documents to prove this - I said, "Keep your hands off Bosnia and Herzegovina." My competencies were so modest and my personal activity and involvement was -- well, I won't go into that. That was a long time ago. But I did my best to prevent the worst from happening, and I failed, thanks in large part to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you are explaining what you said, but as to what I said, you keep saying that I acted otherwise. Just a while ago you said that in 1991 you didn't perform activities that might be termed control of the government of which you were the head, and you were at the head of the government until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In formal terms, yes. But in fact - and I said this in my letter of resignation - the scope of activity for the government, which was small anyway under the constitution, was restricted more and more, to such an extent that in the end there was nothing for the government to do. And I stated this publicly in my letter of resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to what you said in your letter of resignation later on, but this is not relevant for what I'm asking you now. Is it in dispute that throughout 1991 you exercised full activity, meetings with the armed forces, the police, their relevant political factors throughout this time when the sides were arming themselves and there were clashes?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any talks with the army. I don't understand why you're asking me this. What does Mr. Milosevic want?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic wants to say that you had both de facto and de jure authority, that you controlled the federal government up to the end of 1991, while all these events were taking place leading to the break-up of Yugoslavia, and that this can be seen, for example, from your review of the obligations of the president of the Federal Executive Council for 1991, 1990, 1999 [as interpreted], and you can see that there is no difference here. There are no discrepancies. This was all written down in your cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. And then if you're going to put a document to him, you can do so. Now, Mr. Markovic, is there anything you want to add to your previous answer in relation to what the accused is putting to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need to add anything, because the course of events were such that, as I've already said, the Federal Executive Council had very little control or competency or none over the armed forces, and their competencies were restricted more and more. And starting around June 1991, there was hardly any possibility to do anything. We attempted to establish a moratorium, to set up some kind of system for the country to function during the moratorium until the final decision on the fate of Yugoslavia was made. But for this Tribunal, it is not important what the government and its Prime Minister were doing. This is about President Milosevic. And I repeat, he wants to transform the indictment against him into an indictment against me. I ask to be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Markovic, let me explain the process. You have come here to give evidence on very serious offences [Realtime transcript read in error "various areas"] against the accused. Now, he's entitled to defend himself against those charges. And the same with any witness, he's entitled to put his case. Now, you may disagree with it. It may be completely untrue. That doesn't matter. He's entitled to put it. And I would ask you, if you would, please, to deal with him as courteously as I hope you should be dealt with here. This is a trial, and we have to decide ultimately on the guilt or innocence of the accused. So if you would just answer his questions, and if you could do it briefly, so much the better. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes. I wish the transcript would be more accurate. What I said to the witness was not that he had come here to give evidence on various areas. I said he had come to give evidence on serious offences. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we were saying, I have here -- I'm not going to provide it all, but, for example, a review of the obligations of the president of the Federal Executive Council of the Yugoslav government dating back to 1991. This is the original from your cabinet. And we can see the overall activities or, rather, those which were recorded of your activities. And they go on continuously, ending with the 12th of December, 1991 -- 20th of December, 1991, where it says "leave" or "vacation." So this includes your numerous meetings with the army and the police and the Presidency and various political figures, both domestic and foreign, and so on and so forth. So throughout that year of 1991, while Yugoslavia was being broken up, you have a lot of activities, and from all this we cannot conclude that your competencies were limited and restricted in any way. So take a look at this review.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should like to tender it into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, I should like to ask you to tell me when it was that you had this meeting with me in December. When was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with one thing at a time. We're dealing with this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd just like to look for it, because I don't seem to be able to find it, any trace of a meeting where it says "Milosevic." It just doesn't seem to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you remember when it was that you allegedly had a meeting with me in December?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have the beginning of December here. From the beginning of December - and I'm looking through the pages - your agenda, programme of work and the meetings recorded. And there's no record of that meeting with me throughout December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. What are you looking at, Mr. Milosevic? What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is a review of the obligations of the president of the Federal Executive Council in 1991. It was his own cabinet that kept these records, and I got them from the archives of his own cabinet, that is to say, from the federal government. It records each of his meetings. For example, it says, "The 18th of June, 1991, luncheon with S. Milosevic at 1400 hours, Slobodan Milosevic; at 1500 hours, lunch with Milosevic." That was the 18th of June, 1991, for example. So it's that whole day of the 18th. "Telephone, Warren Zimmerman, US ambassador; at 11.00 a.m., Vukotic; 11.45, Murat Galic," and so on and so forth, the agenda. "11.50, agreement with respect to the Slovenian laws, Mitrovic, Maksic, Gracanin, Borovec, Zlokan, Santonaz [phoen], Medjovanovic [phoen], Vajovic, Pecar," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at 1400 hours, Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the idea. Now, let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all your contacts and meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Markovic, if you'd care to look at that. And first of all, tell us if it seems to be an authentic document when you've had a chance to look at it, and then you can also look through December.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] December is at the very end, and it is rather short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is reviewing the document, the Chamber will perhaps have in mind that this is not a document we were able to provide, because archives, of course, have been, in general, completely unavailable to us. But if documents of this kind exist for other organs of the government, in particular for the organs of the accused, we'll be very interested in seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a document -- well, yes, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paper has gone all yellow in the 12 years since. It's the document. Mr. Nice asked about it. It's the document from Mr. Markovic's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? I wasn't able to read through this whole document. It would require much more time. According to what it says, one could say that the document was authentic and that that is what my -- the notes that my cabinet kept with respect to my activities. But we can also see that from July onwards there -- or thereabouts, all the topics of my activities from people who know what all this was about, we can see that this was just within the frameworks of the government. For example, "Friday, the 6th, Tasic, Aco Mitrovic, preparations for The Hague Conference, the flight to The Hague, the meeting in The Hague, internal consultations, interview for Radio B-92, monitoring and so on." All this was internal consultations.
