There weren't any activities which would speak about the functioning of -- functioning outside the building, if I can put it that way, of the Federal Executive Council or Yugoslav government. And let me just add, although it's not important in this context, that I asked to be given from the Federal Executive Council material relating to my work there and a whole library of materials and documents that I worked on during those three years. I was not able to get anything from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you say -- you yourself say that the government is authentic, would you please find this meeting with me in December.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it doesn't -- it's not recorded, but that doesn't mean that the meeting didn't take place. Most probably I didn't verify this, so I didn't check it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your cabinet didn't know where you had gone. You went secretly. You left the cabinet secretly.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way if you want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, the prime minister of the federal government goes to see the president of the Republic of Serbia in the centre of Belgrade secretly, not recorded anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Milosevic, you've made your point. You've heard the answer. No point going over it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you exhibit this, please? And I should like to have the document returned to me once it has been photocopied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to add something, please? I informed Loncar about that conversation. Loncar at the time was the foreign minister. And I mentioned that in a conversation that I had in Trieste with de Michelis also sometime at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document is being spoken of by the accused as if it's an original. If it's an original, then in accordance with your usual policy you should retain the original and he should have the copy. And it will be interesting to know in due course how the yellowed pages of the original come to be in the accused's hands, when, as I say -- whatever it is. But the original we'd like to see as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course you shall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registry will keep the original. You can have a photocopy back. The Registry will keep it. The Prosecution can have a look now. We will give it the next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D207, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I don't have anything against having a photocopy myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, Mr. Markovic, to take a look at this document from the cabinet of the then-Foreign Affairs Minister Loncar about the conversation with the US Secretary of State, James Baker, in 1991, in which it is also clearly set out that the army, under the control -- is under the control of the Presidency and the government, as it states. This, then, otherwise is a document, Mr. May, which the opposite side possesses. It is 064611, the ERN number. And it is titled "The Federal Secretariat for Foreign Affairs, the Cabinet of the Foreign Secretary." It has a confidential number, et cetera, et cetera. I don't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. want to read it out. The date is the 11th of May, 1991. It is a note on the telephone conversation between the federal secretary for foreign affairs, Loncar, with the US Secretary of State, J. Baker. And the note was sent out to the president of the SFRY, the Presidency and the President Jovic; to the president of the Federal Assembly, Gligorijevic; to the president of the Federal Executive Council, Ante Markovic; to the vice-minister of the Federal Defence Secretary, Kadijevic and Gracanin; and then also to certain key figures in the Federal Secretary for Foreign Affairs. It wasn't sent out to anybody in Serbia, just sent out at federal level. And let us take a look at what the third paragraph of the document states. I assume that you provided that to the opposite side over there, because you are mentioned -- or perhaps you didn't provide them with that. Anyway, paragraph 3 says: "In response to Baker's question whether there was the danger of the army acting autonomously or that this should be done by some of its parts, in the area of Croatia, the Federal Secretary Loncar said that the army was under the full control of the Federal Secretary of National Defence and that he was responsible to the Presidency and the government." And then a few lines further on - and you can read that for yourselves, you can read it all, but to save time - it says: "The actions of the army were calculated basically on guaranteeing security to the population and saving them from unrest and conflict, protecting them from unrest and conflict." So that, then, is the government's position and Loncar is discussing this with Baker. Loncar also comes from Croatia -- or rather, he's a Croat from Croatia. He was the foreign minister at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let the witness see the document, and then we must adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you come to look at the document, would you take a look and see that it says quite precisely that the JNA was to be deployed to protect and safeguard the safety of the population, which is what your minister, the minister of foreign affairs, is saying.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a telephone conversation in fact, if I understand it correctly, between Mr. Baker and Mr. Loncar. Now, what Baker and Loncar discussed and who drew up these minutes, I really can't enter into that. At any rate, this is not a document of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll give it the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D208, Your Honour.

Mr. Nice, if you'd like to arrange with the witness a suitable time for him to come back.

utterances.text: We will, and obviously we'll restrict our conversations with him to that topic.
